Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Summary of assessment findings (from transcript and DDx): 
  - Acute insect sting (bee/wasp) occurred minutes before consultation with puncture mark and localized redness on right arm.
  - Patient reports subjective difficulty breathing and odd sensation in lips/tongue but was speaking normally and had no objective airway compromise on remote exam.
  - Clinician judged presentation most consistent with a localized allergic/inflammatory reaction and not currently life-threatening.
  - Clinician advised observation for progression and provided self-care and escalation instructions.
- Diagnostic reasoning (DDx aligned with transcript):
  - Large local allergic reaction / localized urticaria — high likelihood given local puncture mark and localized erythema; clinician identified this as most likely.
  - Early or evolving IgE-mediated anaphylaxis — medium likelihood given temporal onset and subjective airway symptoms; less likely due to absence of objective airway compromise, stridor, hypotension, or widespread urticaria at assessment.
  - Anxiety / panic-related dyspnea — medium likelihood as contributing factor given patient’s history of occasional anxiety and subjective breathlessness despite normal observed breathing.
- Contradictions or unsupported suggestions: None identified

Management Plan
- Acute management provided/recommended:
  - Take an oral antihistamine (examples given by clinician): chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet — can be taken up to six times daily as per clinician’s advice.
  - Alternate option: once-a-day oral antihistamine (unspecified) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - No epinephrine prescribed; no immediate emergency treatment required per clinician’s assessment.
  - Advice to go to Emergency Department immediately if any signs of deterioration: new or worsening difficulty breathing, stridor, progressive lip/tongue swelling, dizziness, collapse, or other systemic features.
  - Monitor sting site for spreading redness, increased warmth, spreading swelling or systemic signs of infection — if these develop, seek medical review (possible need for antibiotics).
  - No routine allergy testing recommended at this time; consider blood testing/allergy referral only if recurrent reactions occur.
- Follow-up: Return or seek urgent care if symptoms worsen; routine GP follow-up if concerns persist or recurrence occurs

Consider:
- Pathology tests as above: Not recorded (clinician noted blood testing may be considered only if recurrent pattern develops)
- EPC referral for allied health (10x visits/year): Not recorded
- Dental referral: Not recorded
- Optometry referral: Not recorded

- Dietitian referral: Not recorded
- CTG registration (if not enrolled): Not recorded

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Large local allergic reaction (localized urticaria/inflammatory reaction to insect sting) — High likelihood
  - Justification: Puncture mark and localized redness/blotchy rash at sting site; no objective airway compromise; clinician and DDx identify this as most likely.
- Early or evolving IgE-mediated anaphylaxis (systemic allergic reaction with possible airway involvement) — Medium likelihood
  - Justification: Symptoms began minutes after sting and patient reports subjective dyspnea and lip/tongue oddness; absence of objective signs (no stridor, normal speech, no hypotension) makes full anaphylaxis less likely at presentation but possible if symptoms evolve.
- Anxiety / panic-related dyspnea — Medium likelihood
  - Justification: Patient admits occasional anxiety and is anxious about progression; objective exam during consultation was reassuring, suggesting a psychological contribution to perceived breathlessness is possible.
